###### Abstract

The introduction of generalist robot policies has enabled a single,
large model to learn to perform a variety of tasks from a vast
pre-training corpus. While these models often exhibit powerful zero-shot
generalization capabilities, they typically require an adaptation phase
to achieve sufficient performance in deployment. Iterated
self-improvement via reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated
promise in enabling this adaptation, yet such approaches have been
largely explored in _single-task_ settings – where the goal is to simply
improve on a narrow deployment task – which lies in stark contrast to
the _multi-task_ capabilities of the base policy. In this work we ask
whether generalist robot policies are capable of multi-task, _generalist
improvement in deployment_ – targeting many diverse tasks simultaneously
– and what algorithmic recipe enables this. To answer this question, we
first develop a set of structured evaluations to test generalist
improvement capabilities, and systematically evaluate algorithmic and
practical design choices regarding value estimation, policy extraction
and resource allocation. We show that not only can generalist policies
be improved online across diverse tasks, but that the right recipe can
enable _generalization_ and increase performance on tasks not considered
during online training. We characterize when this generalization occurs
and show that both the training task distribution and the use of
value-based RL are critical. To the best of our knowledge, this is among
the first evidence for online generalist improvement for robot
foundation models.

## 1 Introduction

Figure 1: Scaling the number of RL training tasks enables generalist
improvement of generalist robot policies. As training task diversity
increases, critic-guided policy extraction (OGPO) or refinement (BoN)
prevent forgetting and improve performance on unseen tasks on
MolmoSpaces, unlike filtered supervised fine-tuning (FSFT).

Generalist robot policies, particularly Vision-Language-Action Models
(VLAs), have shown promise in enabling general-purpose robotic
capabilities, allowing a single policy to be deployed across diverse
tasks ([Brohan et al., 2023](#bib.bib32); [Octo Model Team et al.,
2024](#bib.bib33); [Black et al., 2025](#bib.bib10); [NVIDIA et al.,
2025](#bib.bib17)). However, despite encoding diverse task-solving
behaviors, such policies often lack sufficient reliability for robust
deployment, and a degree of adaptation is typically necessary for
effective performance ([Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib34); [Intelligence et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib14); [Reuss et al., 2025](#bib.bib30)). While
enabling this adaptation through human supervision is often
prohibitively expensive, autonomous adaptation through reinforcement
learning (RL) has emerged as a promising approach to scale policy
improvement, enabling robots to learn from their own experience in
deployment ([Intelligence et al., 2025a](#bib.bib50)). Yet, such
autonomous improvement is typically limited to narrow _single-task_
settings. As such, while these approaches enable generalist policies to
improve, they may also specialize this improvement to the particular
deployment task considered, and achieving improved performance on
additional tasks of interest generally requires further online
interaction and fine-tuning.

A generalist policy, however, can produce a wide range of behaviors
across diverse tasks, even if these behaviors may be far from optimal.
Ideally we might hope that, by deploying on a diverse range of tasks, we
could improve the performance of the policy _across all tasks
simultaneously_ – boosting its performance not just on a single
deployment task, but on the entire distribution of tasks of interest. In
particular, we might hope to enable truly _generalist improvement_:
improvement on both the diverse set of tasks we deploy on, as well as
_generalization_ beyond these deployment tasks and improved performance
on future novel deployment settings. This motivates the central question
we consider in this work: _how can we leverage interaction across a
diverse set of tasks to enable online generalist improvement of
generalist policies?_ That is, can a careful adaptation phase over
multiple tasks enable both (i) improvement across these tasks
simultaneously, and (ii) generalization beyond them, improving
performance on tasks not encountered during post-training?

In this paper, we undertake a systematic study to quantify generalist
policy improvement across different axes of generalization. We show that
appropriate recipes, when instantiated carefully, can enable not only
generalist policy improvement across a diverse set of training tasks,
but also task-generalization – improvement on tasks not seen during
training. Further, we show that this improvement _scales_ with the
number and diversity of tasks trained on, as we showcase in
[Figure 1](#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").
Our results suggest that moving beyond the single-task paradigm is not
only possible but also _crucial_ for achieving broader, generalist
improvement.

We isolate the essential algorithmic ingredients that enable multi-task
learning and generalization. Specifically, we compare three families of
learning approaches:

- (a)
  _Direct Policy Adaptation_, which directly improves the policy via
  filtered supervised fine-tuning on successful trajectories ([Peters
  and Schaal, 2007](#bib.bib36); [Zhou et al., 2024](#bib.bib37); [Qin
  and Springenberg, 2025](#bib.bib38), FSFT,).
- (b)
  _Critic-Guided Test-Time Refinement_, which uses test-time
  optimization against a learned state-action critic to improve actions.
  Here, we focus on Best-of-N sampling  ([Nakamoto et al.,
  2024](#bib.bib39); [Giridhar et al., 2026](#bib.bib40), BoN,) with
  respect to that critic’s induced action ranking as a representative
  recipe.
- (c)
  _Critic-Guided Policy Extraction_, which updates a policy so as to
  maximize the value the critic assigns to the actions produced. Here,
  we adopt off-policy generative policy optimization ([Patil et al.,
  2026](#bib.bib22), OGPO,) as a representative recipe, while also
  ablating alternative approaches such as combining FSFT and BoN
  sampling, or using AWR-inspired policy updates ([Peng et al.,
  2019](#bib.bib25)).

Overall, while all three approaches enable some degree of generalization
given a sufficient diversity in training tasks, we find that
_critic-guided methods enable a substantially greater degree of task
generalization than direct policy adaptation alone_. In particular, we
show that critic-guided methods afford generalization both across
training scenes, and, perhaps more surprisingly, across object types.
Furthermore, we find that critic-guided policy extraction (OGPO)
significantly outperforms test-time refinement (BoN), while also
exhibiting similar scaling trends with training task diversity. This
finding further points to _critic-learning_ as the key component that
enables generalist robotic policy improvement as task diversity scales.

In addition to investigating algorithmic choices, we also systematically
evaluate the training task distribution necessary for achieving such
generalist improvement. We show that both the number of distinct
training tasks, as well as the type of diversity exhibited in these
training tasks, is critical to achieving generalist improvement. In
particular, we find that a high degree of diversity in the required
solution strategies within the training task distribution is crucial to
learning generalizable task-solving behaviors.

We believe these results illustrate a path forward for efficient online
improvement of generalist robot policies. Rather than expensive
single-task improvement on each deployment task of interest, our results
show that, by amortizing this cost across a diverse set of tasks, one
can enable generalist improvement, achieving improved performance on
future deployment tasks of interest without paying the cost of
additional online fine-tuning.

## 2 Related Work

VLA post-training.  Diffusion and flow-matching provide expressive
generative policy classes that, when trained through behavior cloning at
sufficient scale and diversity, can form the basis of generalist
policies ([Janner et al., 2022](#bib.bib6); [Chi et al.,
2023](#bib.bib7); [Reed et al., 2022](#bib.bib47)). Recent RL
fine-tuning methods directly optimize such policies ([Psenka et al.,
2024](#bib.bib29); [Park et al., 2025b](#bib.bib26); [Wagenmaker et al.,
2025](#bib.bib12); [Patil et al., 2026](#bib.bib22); [Li and Levine,
2026](#bib.bib27)), but scaling them to large VLAs remains challenging.
Existing VLA post-training therefore often relies on simpler, readily
scalable methods. One family directly updates the policy using
high-quality experience, including filtered supervised fine-tuning ([Qin
and Springenberg, 2025](#bib.bib38); [Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib24)),
conditioned behavior cloning ([Intelligence et al., 2025a](#bib.bib50)),
and soft variants that weight demonstrations by estimated value ([Peng
et al., 2019](#bib.bib25); [Su et al., 2026](#bib.bib23)). A
complementary family leaves the policy unchanged and instead uses
learned value functions for test-time action selection, such as
Best-of-N ([Nakamoto et al., 2024](#bib.bib39); [Dodeja et al.,
2026](#bib.bib13)), or by learning residual policies to modify the
output action ([Ankile et al., 2025](#bib.bib56); [Dong et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib43); [Xiao et al., 2026](#bib.bib5)) or steer the
pre-trained policy’s denoising process ([Wagenmaker et al.,
2025](#bib.bib12)). We likewise focus on simple, scalable techniques,
demonstrating (cf.
[Section 4](#S4 "4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"))
that they can achieve competitive performance. While these existing
approaches to VLA post-training have demonstrated performance
gains ([Zhang et al., 2024](#bib.bib53); [Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib55);
[Ankile et al., 2025](#bib.bib56); [Myers et al., 2024](#bib.bib60); [Li
et al., 2025](#bib.bib51); [Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib54); [Dong et
al., 2026b](#bib.bib57); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib58); [Lu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib59); [Sun and Song, 2025](#bib.bib52)), they are limited,
primarily, to improvement on single, individual tasks ([Xu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib15); [Pan et al., 2026b](#bib.bib16); [NVIDIA et al.,
2025](#bib.bib17); [Team et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)). In contrast, we
study joint post-training across increasingly broad task distributions
and ask whether the resulting policy also improves on tasks outside the
training distribution.

Multi-task generalization.  A separate literature studies how robotic
performance scales with the diversity of training tasks. Prior work
considers multi-task scaling without foundation-model policies ([Nauman
et al., 2025](#bib.bib18)), while meta-reinforcement learning instead
develops algorithms that _learn to rapidly adapt_ to unseen tasks
(rather than to directly transfer a fixed policy to new tasks, the
setting we consider), traditionally with relatively small
policies ([Duan et al., 2016](#bib.bib61); [Finn et al.,
2017](#bib.bib62); [Yu et al., 2019](#bib.bib63)). More recent work
extends this perspective to VLA policies through behavior
cloning ([Bianchi et al., 2026](#bib.bib64)). Other works study
generalization arising from scaling behavior cloning during
pretraining ([Zheng et al., 2026](#bib.bib19); [Dyna Robotics,
2026](#bib.bib68)) or post-training ([Lin et al., 2025](#bib.bib4); [Lin
et al., 2026](#bib.bib20)). Here we focus on self-improvement via
reinforcement learning. Perhaps closest to our setting is [Liu et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib21), who compare generalization of offline SFT from
expert demonstrations with on-policy reinforcement-learning algorithms
such as PPO ([Schulman et al., 2017](#bib.bib41)) and GRPO ([Shao et
al., 2024](#bib.bib42)). Our study differs in two important ways. First,
[Liu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib21) utilize a single fixed distribution over
training environments for all experiments; in contrast, a primary
contribution of our work is quantifying which training distributions are
necessary to induce generalization. Second, while we consider standard
online RL fine-tuning procedures commonly used for VLAs, and study which
such fine-tuning procedures enable generalization, this work compares
non-RL approaches (SFT on expert demonstrations) to on-policy RL. While
[Liu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib21) show that RL fine-tuning can enable
greater generalization than SFT, our work provides informative guidance
as to which design decisions are key to enabling this in practice. We
note as well that multi-task generalization in post-training has been
long studied in LLM post-training. We refer to
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Extended Related Work ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
where we draw parallels to this work.

## 3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology

### 3.1 Problem Setting: Generalist Improvement of Generalist Policies

We model our environment as a contextual Markov decision process
$`\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{C},P,R,\mu_{0},\gamma)`$,
where $`\mathcal{S}`$ and $`\mathcal{A}`$ are continuous state and
action spaces, $`\mathcal{C}`$ is a space of contexts encoding different
tasks¹¹ 1 In practice, a task will correspond to following a specific
prompt in a specific manipulation environment.,
$`P:\mathcal{S\times A\times C}\to\Delta(\mathcal{S})`$ is a stochastic
transition function,
$`R:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{C}\to[R_{\min},R_{\max}]`$
is a context-conditional reward function specifying each task,
$`\mu_{0}:\mathcal{C}\to\Delta(\mathcal{S})`$ is an initial distribution
and $`\gamma\in[0,1)`$ is a discount factor. We model a generalist agent
as a context-conditional policy
$`\pi:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{C}\to\Delta(\mathcal{A})`$²² 2 We
overload notation and condition $`\pi`$ on $`c\in\mathcal{C}`$ for
simplicity; in practice, if $`\pi`$ is a VLA, the task conditioning is
provided in the form of a language command, and the policy outputs
action chunks., and evaluate its expected return from a state-action
pair $`(s,a)`$ and task $`c`$ according to its Q-function:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\textstyle Q^{\pi}(s,a,c)=\mathbb{E}_{P,\pi,c}\left[\sum_{t\geq 0}\gamma^{t}R(s_{t},a_{t},c)\mid s_{0}=s,a_{0}=a\right],\;\;
``` |  | (1) |

where above, $`\mathbb{E}_{P,\pi,c}`$ denotes expectation with respect
to
$`a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\,|\,s_{t},c)\;\text{and}\;s_{t+1}\sim P(\cdot\,|\,s_{t},a_{t},c)`$.
We denote
$`V^{\pi}(s,c)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi(\cdot\,|\,s,c)}[Q^{\pi}(s,a,c)]`$.

In this work, we are interested in enabling improvement on tasks from
some test distribution $`\rho_{\mathrm{test}}\in\Delta(\mathcal{C})`$,
which may or may not correspond to the training distribution. We refer
to this setting as generalist improvement of generalist policies (or
generalist improvement for brevity). Given a task distribution
$`\rho_{\mathrm{test}}`$, the objective of generalist improvement of
generalist policies is to update $`\pi`$ so as to maximize:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\textstyle J(\pi;\rho_{\mathrm{test}})=\mathbb{E}_{c\sim\rho_{\mathrm{test}},s_{0}\sim\mu_{0}(c)}\left[V^{\pi}(s_{0},c)\right].
``` |  | (2) |

Generalist improvement protocol.  In this work we assume we are given
some initial generalist policy $`\pi_{\mathrm{gen}}`$, achieving
non-zero but imperfect zero-shot success across tasks, and that we can
interact online with a set of training tasks drawn from a distribution
$`\rho_{\mathrm{train}}`$. As stated, our goal is to learn a fine-tuned
policy $`\pi_{\mathrm{ft}}`$ that maximizes
$`J(\pi_{\mathrm{ft}};\rho_{\mathrm{test}})`$. Crucially,
$`\rho_{\mathrm{test}}`$ need not coincide with
$`\rho_{\mathrm{train}}`$, in which case the policy must generalize to
tasks it was not trained on. At the same time, these two distributions
need to be related (see
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.3 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")),
as generalization to arbitrary tasks is in practice unrealistic (see
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Generalist improvement on LIBERO: does generalization occur for completely novel tasks? ‣ Appendix C Additional Empirical Results ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"),
 [Yu et al., 2020](#bib.bib35) and  [Malik et al. (2021)](#bib.bib74)).
For simplicity, we will assume that $`\rho_{\mathrm{train}}`$ is
supported on a finite set of tasks
$`[c_{1},\ldots,c_{N_{\mathrm{task}}}]`$. We consider interaction with
the training tasks through repeated iterations $`m=1,\ldots,M`$, each
involving online interaction and training. For each iteration $`m`$, we
first collect $`K`$
episodes $`\tau_{1,1:K},\dots,\tau_{N_{\mathrm{task}},1:K}`$ from each
training task $`[c_{1},\dots,c_{N_{\mathrm{task}}}]`$, with the policy
frozen, and then update the policy given the newly collected experience.
This protocol approaches traditional, single-task online RL by choosing
$`\rho_{\mathrm{train}}=\rho_{\mathrm{test}}`$ and setting $`K=1`$, and
tends towards multi-task offline RL ([Dong et al., 2026b](#bib.bib57),
or “batch online RL”,) when a single iteration is applied ($`M=1`$,
$`K\gg 1`$) and $`\rho_{\mathrm{train}}`$ has larger support. To
simulate realistic fleet-level robot deployments, we choose a moderately
large $`K`$ and $`M`$, discussed
in [Section C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Allocating resources: data and compute ‣ Appendix C Additional Empirical Results ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").
We visualize the protocol in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Problem Setting: Generalist Improvement of Generalist Policies ‣ 3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 2: Generalist improvement and evaluation. (1) A generalist policy
collects $`K`$ rollouts $`\tau_{n,k}`$ across training tasks
$`c_{n}\sim\rho_{\mathrm{train}}`$. (2) Task-specific experience is
pooled in a shared replay buffer and used to enact one of three families
of methods: direct policy adaptation updates the policy according to
success labels, critic-guided refinement learns critics for action
ranking, and critic-guided policy extraction learns critics and updates
the policy towards actions with high critic values. This process is
iterated $`M`$ times. (3) Evaluation is carried out over training tasks
($`c\sim\rho_{\mathrm{train}}`$), as well as on unseen test tasks
($`c\sim\rho_{\mathrm{test}}`$) to test generalization.

### 3.2 Mechanisms for Generalist Improvement

In this work, we aim to understand what algorithmic approaches enable
generalist improvement. We distinguish between two complementary and
independent mechanisms for policy improvement: direct policy adaptation,
which updates the parameters of the robot policy alone, and
critic-guided refinement, which instead learns a value function to
“grade” robot actions. We consider approaches that isolate each of these
components (FSFT, BoN), in order to determine which mechanism drives
generalist improvement, as well as representative approaches that
combine both (in particular, we primarily consider OGPO). We emphasize
that the focus of this work is not primarily developing novel
algorithms, but rather understanding whether existing techniques for
policy learning can enable generalist improvement. We therefore focus on
existing paradigmatic approaches. We defer specific implementation
details of the algorithms described below to Appendix
[D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix D Experimental Details ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").

Direct policy adaptation. As a representative and scalable approach to
direct policy adaptation, we consider weighted supervised learning. At
each iteration, we sample a batch of state-action-task tuples from the
buffer, and define a weighting function
$`w:\mathcal{S\times A\times C}\to\mathbb{R}`$ in order to minimize a
weighted negative log-likelihood under the policy:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPA}}(\theta)=-\,\mathbb{E}_{(s,a,c)\sim\mathcal{D}}\big[w(s,a,c)\log\pi_{\theta}(a|s,c)\big],
``` |  | (3) |

for policy parameters $`\theta`$. When an explicit likelihood is not
available, a tractable lower bound can be adopted (e.g., the flow
matching loss in the case of modern VLAs ([Intelligence et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib14))). The simplest instantiation of this mechanism is
referred to as %-BC ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib8)) or filtered
supervised fine-tuning ([Zhou et al., 2024](#bib.bib37), FSFT,), which
sets $`w(s_{t},a_{t},c)=\mathbf{1}_{G(s_{t},a_{t},c)>G_{\min}}`$ where
$`G(s_{t},a_{t},c)=\sum_{t^{\prime}\geq t}R(s_{t^{\prime}},a_{t^{\prime}},c)`$
is the empirical return, and $`G_{\min}`$ a threshold. This mechanism
implements a form of policy improvement ([Qin and Springenberg,
2025](#bib.bib38)) while isolating the policy update mechanism and
conveniently remaining as close as possible to a purely supervised
objective. We thus adopt FSFT as our paradigmatic approach for direct
policy adaptation; we nevertheless also consider approaches that set
$`w(s,a,c)`$ based on a learned value function in
Section [4.4.3](#S4.SS4.SSS3 "4.4.3 Recipes for Policy Extraction ‣ 4.4 Q4: What enables generalist policy improvement? ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").

Critic-guided test-time refinement. Orthogonally to direct policy
adaptation, improvement can also occur through utilizing a learned value
function. We consider training a parametric state-action critic
$`Q_{\psi}`$ to estimate the state-action value function expressed in
Equation [1](#S3.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ 3.1 Problem Setting: Generalist Improvement of Generalist Policies ‣ 3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").
While many approaches for value estimation exist (and are ablated in
Section [4.4.2](#S4.SS4.SSS2 "4.4.2 What Makes a Good Value Function in VLA Post-Training? ‣ 4.4 Q4: What enables generalist policy improvement? ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")),
we find that training $`Q_{\psi}`$ together with a state value function
$`V_{\eta}`$ through the following standard temporal difference (TD)
learning update performs reliably:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\textstyle\mathcal{L}_{Q}(\psi)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{(s,a,r,s^{\prime},c)\sim\mathcal{D}}\Big[\big(Q_{\psi}(s,a,c)-(r+\gamma V_{\eta}(s^{\prime},c))\big)^{2}\Big]\quad\text{and}\quad`$ |  | (4) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\textstyle\mathcal{L}_{V}(\eta)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{(s,a,c)\sim\mathcal{D}}\Big[\big(Q_{\psi}(s,a,c)-V_{\eta}(s,c)\big)^{2}\Big].`$ |  | (5) |

We refer to
Section [4.4.2](#S4.SS4.SSS2 "4.4.2 What Makes a Good Value Function in VLA Post-Training? ‣ 4.4 Q4: What enables generalist policy improvement? ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
for ablations of our critic-learning objective (e.g., Monte Carlo
returns and distributional critics). As our goal is to understand the
mechanisms that enable generalist improvement, we wish to isolate the
contribution of policy adaptation from critic refinement. To achieve
this, we build on a long line of works on test-time action
selection ([Kalashnikov et al., 2018](#bib.bib44)) that guide the policy
via Best-of-N (BoN) sampling ([Nakamoto et al., 2024](#bib.bib39)). In
particular, we keep the policy parameters frozen and re-rank sampled
actions at test-time according to their estimated values. That is, for a
task $`c`$ and the current state $`s_{t}`$ in a rollout, we draw $`N`$
action candidates $`\{a_{t}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}\sim\pi_{\theta}(s_{t},c)`$,
score them and execute action chunk $`a_{t}^{i^{\star}}`$ with

|     |                                                             |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       i^{\star}=\arg\max_{i}Q_{\mathrm{targ}}(s_{t},a_{t}^{i},c).
       ```                                                          |     | (6) |

where $`Q_{\mathrm{targ}}`$ is a target critic network ([Lillicrap et
al., 2016](#bib.bib45)) derived from $`Q_{\psi}`$ (see
[Section D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix D Experimental Details ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
for details). This allows online experience to influence behavior
through action selection while preserving the policy parameters
inherited from pre-training; moreover, despite its simplicity, we found
this recipe to perform reliably in practice (see
Section [4](#S4 "4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")).

Critic-guided policy extraction.  Lastly, we consider a third approach
to policy improvement: updating the base policy so as to maximize the
value the learned critic assigns to its actions ([Peng et al.,
2019](#bib.bib25); [Lillicrap et al., 2016](#bib.bib45)). Formally,
rather than simply using the critic to select actions from the base
policy as in Equation
[6](#S3.E6 "Equation 6 ‣ 3.2 Mechanisms for Generalist Improvement ‣ 3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"),
we *train* the policy to produce actions with large critic values, for
example, maximizing an objective of the form:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CPE}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(s,c)\sim\mathcal{D}}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s,c)}[Q_{\mathrm{targ}}(s,a)].
``` |  | (7) |

As a representative recipe, we focus on off-policy generative policy
optimization ([Patil et al., 2026](#bib.bib22), OGPO,). Specifically,
OGPO is targeted at generative control policies ([Chi et al.,
2023](#bib.bib7); [Pan et al., 2026a](#bib.bib1)), such as flow-policies
([Black et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)), which produce actions via a sequence
of denoising steps. OGPO alternates between training a critic on
observed transitions, using an update similar to Equation
[4](#S3.E4 "Equation 4 ‣ 3.2 Mechanisms for Generalist Improvement ‣ 3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"),
and updating the generative control policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$ to maximize
(Equation
[7](#S3.E7 "Equation 7 ‣ 3.2 Mechanisms for Generalist Improvement ‣ 3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")),
applying a PPO-like update ([Schulman et al., 2017](#bib.bib41)) to the
action generation process to shift its generated actions towards higher
critic values (see
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B A Taxonomy of Post-Training Algorithms ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
for a detailed description).

In addition to OGPO, we ablate against two other approaches to
critic-guided policy extraction: (i) FSFT+BoN, which adapts the policy
with $`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPA}}`$ and filters action at test-time
according to a critic trained with $`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Q/V}}`$, and
(ii) flow-based advantage-weighted regression ([Peng et al.,
2019](#bib.bib25), AWR,), where we use critic-derived estimates of the
advantage function to reweight the supervised learning loss following
Equation
[3](#S3.E3 "Equation 3 ‣ 3.2 Mechanisms for Generalist Improvement ‣ 3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").
We evaluate each in
Section [4.4.3](#S4.SS4.SSS3 "4.4.3 Recipes for Policy Extraction ‣ 4.4 Q4: What enables generalist policy improvement? ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
and provide full details in
Appendices [B](#A2 "Appendix B A Taxonomy of Post-Training Algorithms ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
and [D](#A4 "Appendix D Experimental Details ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").

### 3.3 Experimental Setup

Our experiments are designed to answer the following core questions:

- •
  Q1: As the diversity of training tasks increases, how effective are
  the three representative recipes (direct policy adaptation,
  critic-guided test-time refinement and critic-guided policy
  extraction) at driving self-improvement on the tasks they are exposed
  to?
- •
  Q2: To what extent and at which scale does either mechanism generalize
  to unseen tasks?
- •
  Q3: What is the nature of the observed generalization, and in which
  cases is it most effective?
- •
  Q4: Which specific algorithmic design choices drive learning within
  and beyond the training task distribution, i.e., enable generalist
  improvement?

To answer these questions, we design a post-training and evaluation
protocol centered on directly controlling the training and test task
distributions $`\rho_{\mathrm{train}}`$ and $`\rho_{\mathrm{test}}`$
introduced in
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Problem Setting: Generalist Improvement of Generalist Policies ‣ 3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 3: Objects and scenes in MolmoSpaces. Left: 4 tasks covering two
objects, each with two scenes. Center: unseen scenes of the training
objects. Right: examples of unseen objects.

Training environments.  To answer Q1 and Q2, we consider training
distributions that differ in both the number of distinct tasks and their
diversity. We base our evaluation on the MolmoSpaces ([Kim et al.,
2026](#bib.bib3)) benchmark, which gives precise control over task
diversity. We focus on the pick suite, which instructs the agent to
grasp and lift various objects in different domestic environments. This
benchmark exposes 18 task objects and 55-56 scenes per object (e.g., the
“fork” object spans 56 distinct scenes); we visualize examples in
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.3 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").
This enables task variation along multiple axes: scene variation, which
is primarily visual in nature, and object variation, which generally
alters the grasping strategy necessary to successfully solve the task.
In our main evaluation
(Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")),
we consider training task distributions over growing numbers of tasks,
from $`1`$ to $`144`$, spanning different objects and scenes. Each set
of tasks is procedurally selected to be a superset of smaller sets,
while maintaining the same non-zero average performance of the base
policy over tasks ($`{\approx}30\%`$). This ensures that larger sets of
tasks are at least as diverse as smaller ones, as they cannot include
fewer objects and scenes. Additional evaluations, e.g., in
Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.2 Q2: Do we see generalization beyond training tasks? ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"),
ablate the diversity in the set of training tasks, which may only vary
in terms of scenes, or also in terms of objects. We additionally
evaluate on the popular LIBERO ([Liu et al., 2023](#bib.bib2))
manipulation suite, for which tasks are sampled from the LIBERO-90
subset.

Evaluation tasks.  To address Q1, we evaluate policy performance with
respect to the training task distribution
($`\rho_{\mathrm{test}}=\rho_{\mathrm{train}}`$). To address Q2, we
largely leverage MolmoSpaces’s structured task diversity, varying task
novelty across both the axes of task objects and scenes, described above
and depicted in
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.3 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").
Similarly, we evaluate both training and unseen tasks in LIBERO to
assess generalization capability when task diversity cannot be easily
controlled. For a full description of task sets in MolmoSpaces we refer
to
Appendix [D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Environments and Task Splits ‣ Appendix D Experimental Details ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").
In all experiments, we report the final mean success rate over three
training seeds and 95% bootstrap CIs; see
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Training curves ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
for training curves.

Base model, critic architecture, and policy improvement protocol. 
Across experiments, we use the $`\pi_{0.5}`$ VLA ([Intelligence et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib14)) as the base generalist policy
$`\pi_{\mathrm{gen}}`$, in its droid and libero checkpoints for
MolmoSpaces and LIBERO, respectively. Method-specific hyperparameters
are optimized individually, and main results are stated for the
best-performing hyperparameters for each approach. We briefly recap them
here, and present detailed allocation studies and ablations justifying
these decisions in
Section [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Q4: What enables generalist policy improvement? ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
and
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Additional Empirical Results ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").
We implement our critic networks as BroNet ([Nauman et al.,
2024](#bib.bib48)) residual MLPs whose input is the concatenation of
the $`\pi_{0.5}`$ prefix representation, mean-pooled over the prefix
token sequence, the proprioceptive state, and the flattened action
chunk. We use an ensemble of  $`Q`$ and $`V`$-heads and aggregate them
by taking the minimum ([Fujimoto et al., 2018](#bib.bib75)), both when
forming the TD target
in [Equation 4](#S3.E4 "In 3.2 Mechanisms for Generalist Improvement ‣ 3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
and when scoring candidate actions at inference time
via [Equation 6](#S3.E6 "In 3.2 Mechanisms for Generalist Improvement ‣ 3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").
In each experiment, we apply $`M=10`$ iterations of policy improvement,
collecting $`K=20`$ episodes per task per epoch; we find that task
performance does not improve much for larger $`K`$ and $`M`$, as we
report in
Appendix [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Allocating resources: data and compute ‣ Appendix C Additional Empirical Results ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").
For direct policy adaptation, we fine-tune policies for $`100`$ gradient
steps in single-task settings, and $`500`$ gradient steps in multi-task
settings due to greater data scale and variability. In the case of
critic-guided test-time refinement, the critic MLPs, being both smaller
and trained from scratch, are trained with $`100\times`$ gradient steps
(reaching convergence, and roughly matching the training cost of policy
adaptation). We found methods relying on critic-guided policy extraction
to prefer a different allocation of gradient steps (fewer critic updates
with off-policy targets, and more policy updates, as detailed in
Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix D Experimental Details ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")).

We ensure reproducibility by open-sourcing our full pipeline at this
[repository](https://github.com/lasgroup/generalist-improvement).

## 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity

Figure 4: Value-based generalist improvement generalizes beyond the
training tasks. Final success rate on training tasks (left) and held-out
tasks (center and right, unseen scenes and objects) in MolmoSpaces as
the number of distinct training tasks increases (x-axis). BoN and OGPO
display stronger generalization. We report the mean and 95% stratified
bootstrap CIs across three seeds.

We seek to answer our four core questions about generalist policy
improvement. Our analysis centers on
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"),
in which each point corresponds to a training split of $`k`$ objects
with $`k`$ scenes each, evaluated on its own training tasks (left), on
eight unseen scenes of each of its $`k`$ training objects (center), and
on a fixed set of six unseen objects with eight scenes each (right).
Appendix [D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Environments and Task Splits ‣ Appendix D Experimental Details ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
lists every split in full.

### 4.1 Q1: Can we enable generalist improvement on training tasks?

Figure 5: Compute efficiency of generalist improvement. Post-training a
policy on multiple tasks at once achieves the performance of
post-trained single-task experts in significantly fewer gradient steps.

The left panel of
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
evaluates to what extent post-training can improve performance on the
tasks sampled from the training task distribution. For FSFT, BoN and
OGPO, we observe that success rate increases with respect to the base
policy, and generalist improvement succeeds. We find OGPO and BoN to be
generally more effective than FSFT in the single-task setting, where
they lead by $`+53`$ pp and $`+26`$ pp, respectively. As the number of
training tasks increases, we find that in the multi-task setting OGPO
and BoN outperform FSFT by $`+43`$–$`50`$ pp and $`+15`$–$`21`$ pp,
respectively. Neither of the recipes displays fully convincing
cross-task expertise: while potentially overfitting to a specific task,
the average performance of single-task experts (represented as the
leftmost point on these curves) slightly exceeds that of multi-task
policies. We observe similar trends on training tasks for LIBERO, in
which the performance gap with respect to single-task experts is perhaps
more marked – see Appendix
[C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Generalist improvement on LIBERO: does generalization occur for completely novel tasks? ‣ Appendix C Additional Empirical Results ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").
We note, however, that generalist improvement nevertheless holds a
computational edge over post-training single-task experts, as we display
in Figure
[5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.1 Q1: Can we enable generalist improvement on training tasks? ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"):
with a matched data collection budget, a single BoN post-training run
over 16 tasks requires $`2.9\times`$ fewer gradient steps than 16
single-task runs to achieve similar multi-task performance improvements.
Thus, even on in-distribution training tasks, generalist improvement
enables more efficient improvement than single-task training.

### 4.2 Q2: Do we see generalization beyond training tasks?

A different pattern emerges when, instead of measuring performance on
the tasks we train on, we turn to evaluating success rate on unseen
tasks in MolmoSpaces. In this setting, we find, to the best of our
knowledge, one of the first examples of generalization in VLA RL
post-training at this scale. As shown
in [Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
(center and right), single-task post-training leads to forgetting on
unseen objects, and yields at most modest gains on unseen scenes – while
we can improve on the task we train on, performance often degrades on
others.

Figure 6: Diversification transfers better along its own axis. OGPO
success rate when scaling scenes of a single object, or objects with one
scene each, evaluated on eight unseen scenes (left) and eight unseen
objects (right). Each axis transfers best along itself, though only
scaling objects surpasses the base policy on both. Mean and 95%
stratified bootstrap CIs over three seeds.

However, as we increase the number of training tasks, critic-based
recipes (OGPO and BoN) exhibit a transition from forgetting to
generalization. Specifically, we observe performance gains over the base
policy of up to $`+58`$ pp for tasks where the object remains consistent
but the scene changes from the training task, and $`+39`$ pp for tasks
where the object also changes. This indicates that OGPO and BoN can even
handle different objects altogether (e.g., picking up a knife after
training only on other items, such as ladles, pots, and cups, as we
further analyze in the next section). More generally, these results
highlight that post-training VLAs on sufficiently diverse tasks can
yield improvements beyond the training distribution. Indeed, this
generalization *scales with the number of training tasks* – the more
tasks we train on, the greater the generalization benefit – as long as
the correct algorithmic approach is applied. In particular, this
improvement is much more pronounced for OGPO and BoN than FSFT,
demonstrating that critic-guided policy extraction or refinement is
critical for enabling generalization. Together, this suggests that an
effective recipe for generalist improvement is to (i) apply critic-based
policy improvement while (ii) scaling the number of tasks we RL
post-train on. We additionally evaluate generalization in LIBERO in
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Generalist improvement on LIBERO: does generalization occur for completely novel tasks? ‣ Appendix C Additional Empirical Results ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"),
in which we find that this benchmark presents a much greater challenge
in terms of generalization, as inter-task variability is extreme: in
this case, similar patterns occur, but only in terms of forgetting.

### 4.3 Q3: What Is the Nature of the Observed Generalization?

We next carefully analyze which training task splits are most critical
for enabling generalization, and which types of generalization we might
expect a given set of training tasks to induce.

Scaling training objects is critical for generalist improvement. We
first isolate the two axes – scene and object – of task diversity. In
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
they grow together: a split with $`k^{2}`$ tasks contains $`k`$ objects
with $`k`$ scenes each. In this experiment, we instead vary the number
of scenes of a single object, and separately the number of objects with
one scene each. Both are evaluated on eight unseen objects, and on eight
unseen scenes of the object whose scenes the first sweep scales (details
and results for all recipes in
Appendix [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Extended Scaling Task Diversity Ablation ‣ Appendix C Additional Empirical Results ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")).
As shown in
Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.2 Q2: Do we see generalization beyond training tasks? ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"),
we observe earlier generalization to new scenes by training on more
diverse scenes, and greater generalization to new objects by training on
more diverse objects. The two are not symmetric: scaling objects enables
the post-trained policy to surpass the base policy on both unseen
objects and scenes, whereas scaling scenes hardly exceeds it on unseen
objects, even with 16 scenes. This suggests that, to achieve
generalization to novel manipulation strategies (e.g., the grasp
mechanics required to handle a new object), it is necessary to train on
tasks involving diverse manipulation strategies, while robustness over
the scene layout and appearance is easier to achieve.

Figure 7: MolmoSpaces. Final success rate on each of the 6 unseen
objects, none of which appears in any training split, as a function of
the number of training tasks. Points show the mean over three seeds with
95% stratified bootstrap CIs.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![Refer to caption](2611.06905v1/generalization_depicted_variant_4.png)

Figure 8: Generalization across objects. Left: Training objects per
MolmoSpaces split. Each split contains all objects of the previous one;
$`+`$ marks objects added. The 1-task split is trained separately on a
single *box* or *spatula* task. Full task details are in
Table [3](#A4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ D.1 Environments and Task Splits ‣ Appendix D Experimental Details ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").
Right: We train each method on tasks involving a single object (box or
spatula) and evaluate on the unseen knife. For methods that use a critic
(BoN, OGPO), training on a similar object transfers better, whereas FSFT
shows no such pattern. We report the mean and 95% stratified bootstrap
CIs across three seeds.

Critic learning enables generalization on unseen objects that resemble
training objects.
Figure [8](#S4.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 4.3 Q3: What Is the Nature of the Observed Generalization? ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
illustrates this directly: for BoN, training on a similarly shaped
object transfers better (e.g., boxes to bowls, spatulas to knives),
whereas FSFT shows no such pattern. The per-object results
(Figure [7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4.3 Q3: What Is the Nature of the Observed Generalization? ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"))
show the same trend at scale. BoN improves on atomizers and wine bottles
mainly at 144 tasks (atomizer $`0.29{\rightarrow}0.42`$, wine bottle
$`0.24{\rightarrow}0.44`$), the split that adds bottle-like objects such
as soap dispensers and salt/pepper shakers
(Figure [8](#S4.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 4.3 Q3: What Is the Nature of the Observed Generalization? ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"),
left). Forks and knives show substantial improvement with OGPO when we
move from 1 to 4 tasks; at 4 tasks each training split contains
spatulas, which require similar grasping motion to forks and knives; we
believe this enables this generalization. The performance on forks and
knives plateaus at 64 tasks, however. We hypothesize this is because the
objects added between 64 and 144 tasks do not exhibit significant
similarity to forks and knives. OGPO shows a similar pattern on
atomizers ($`0.42{\rightarrow}0.58`$) but not on wine bottles
($`0.09{\rightarrow}0.12`$), while FSFT improves on neither. Since BoN
keeps the policy frozen, the critic alone suffices to transfer to
similar objects, while policy updates alone do not. Across all objects,
we see that critic learning is essential to generalization—with the
exception of bowls, we observe substantial generalization only when
applying critic learning.

Policy updates help on some objects but degrade performance on others.
FSFT and OGPO both improve on some objects (e.g., bowls) but degrade on
wine bottles, where both fall sharply below the base policy while BoN
recovers to about 0.44 at 144 tasks. We find that policy updates can
enable more effective generalization to objects similar to those in the
training distribution (e.g., OGPO on forks), while leading to poor
generalization and even forgetting on objects further from the training
distribution (e.g. wine bottles). In contrast, critic-only updates can
enable effective generalization even on objects far from the training
distribution (e.g., BoN on wine bottle).

### 4.4 Q4: What enables generalist policy improvement?

Having evaluated our recipes at scale, we now validate key design
decisions for multi-task VLA post-training, and investigate several
alternative techniques for critic-guided policy extraction; see
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Additional Empirical Results ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
for additional ablations including data/compute scaling and resource
allocation.

Figure 9: Recipe ablations. Left: full VLA vs. expert-only tuning for
FSFT on MolmoSpaces (64 tasks). Full tuning is essential in-distribution
and on unseen scenes, but degrades most on unseen objects. Center:
architecture for BoN. Right: TD vs MC, classification vs regression for
BoN. Center and right are evaluated on LIBERO (4 tasks; see
Table [4](#A4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ D.1 Environments and Task Splits ‣ Appendix D Experimental Details ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"))
and the object-diverse MolmoSpaces (8 objects, 1 scene each; see
Table [1](#A3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ C.2 Extended Scaling Task Diversity Ablation ‣ Appendix C Additional Empirical Results ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")).

#### 4.4.1 What Makes Direct Policy Adaptation Effective?

An important fine-tuning decision concerns which parameters to update:
the entire VLA or only the action expert, i.e., the flow model mapping
tokens from the backbone to continuous actions. We compare both settings
for FSFT on the MolmoSpaces (64 tasks) split, evaluating
in-distribution, on unseen scenes, and on strongly OOD unseen objects.
The left panel of
Figure [9](#S4.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ 4.4 Q4: What enables generalist policy improvement? ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
shows that *full VLA fine-tuning is beneficial*: it outperforms
expert-only tuning by more than $`+12`$ pp both in-distribution and on
unseen scenes, whereas expert-only tuning improves only marginally over
the base policy. This comes at a cost: on unseen objects, full VLA
tuning degrades performance by $`10.6`$ pp relative to the base policy,
against $`-2.2`$ pp for expert-only tuning. This suggests that full
fine-tuning increases overfitting risks. The two settings therefore
trade in-distribution gains against OOD performance.

Figure 10: Policy extraction schemes. We compare OGPO ([Patil et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22)) to AWR ([Peng et al., 2019](#bib.bib25)) and a direct
combination of FSFT and BoN. We find that natively actor-critic
algorithms perform best.

#### 4.4.2 What Makes a Good Value Function in VLA Post-Training?

Value function learning admits many possible implementations. To find a
scalable recipe for multi-task VLA post-training, we conduct controlled
ablations along multiple design axes, focusing on training-tasks
improvement. We will use BoN as a representative algorithm, arguably
being the simplest recipe involving a critic.
[Figure 9](#S4.F9 "In 4.4 Q4: What enables generalist policy improvement? ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
(center, right) compares two network architectures, regression and
classification objectives, as well as TD and MC targets. Compared to
standard MLP critics, adding residual connections ([Nauman et al.,
2024](#bib.bib48), BroNet;) increases performance by more than
$`+10`$ pp. Regarding the training objective, combining TD targets with
a simple regression loss yields the largest and most consistent
improvements in our experiments. Notably, we find distributional critic
formulations to scale poorly to multi-task settings; we hypothesize this
is due to return distributions of different tasks varying significantly.
Finally, BoN introduces one further hyperparameter, the number of
sampled candidates $`N`$. We ablate its impact on performance and
inference time in
Appendix [C.6](#A3.SS6 "C.6 Number of action candidates 𝑁 in Best-of-𝑁 ‣ Appendix C Additional Empirical Results ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"),
and use $`N=32`$ throughout.

#### 4.4.3 Recipes for Policy Extraction

Through our experiments, we find that OGPO ([Patil et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22)) largely retains the generalization properties of BoN
while enabling expressive policy extraction, and therefore reaches
significantly higher performance.

As such, OGPO, and critic-guided policy extraction in general, can be
interpreted as the combination of the other two mechanisms, namely
direct policy adaptation and critic-guided test-time refinement, where
the latter is applied at training time instead. OGPO is, however, one of
many ways in which this combination can be instantiated. We thus ablate
two alternatives in
Figure [10](#S4.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ 4.4.1 What Makes Direct Policy Adaptation Effective? ‣ 4.4 Q4: What enables generalist policy improvement? ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").
As a straightforward instantiation, we consider FSFT+BoN, which
simultaneously fine-tunes the policy on successful rollouts and trains a
critic for inference-time action selection. We also evaluate
advantage-weighted regression  ([Peng et al., 2019](#bib.bib25), AWR;),
a popular technique which weights the objective in
Equation [3](#S3.E3 "Equation 3 ‣ 3.2 Mechanisms for Generalist Improvement ‣ 3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
by exponentiated advantages, thus implementing a form of regularized
policy improvement. We find that all three schemes are effective. Yet,
OGPO and AWR generally outperform a straightforward combination of FSFT
and BoN; we hypothesize this is due to a finer implementation of policy
improvement.

## 5 Discussion

This work studies the adaptation regimes of generalist policies as the
diversity of their set of fine-tuning tasks increases. We isolate three
techniques for self-improvement, centered respectively on updating the
policy parameters, on training value estimates and refining actions at
test-time, and on extracting a better policy according to those value
estimates. While all mechanisms improve performance on training tasks,
we find that, at a sufficient scale, value-based RL is instrumental in
inducing a degree of generalization beyond observed tasks, and in
achieving generalist improvement of generalist policies. We believe
these results show a promising way forward for efficiently improving
generalist robot policies, moving beyond expensive single-task
improvement to enable improvement through generalization on diverse
training tasks.

Limitations.   Our contributions are empirical in nature. As such, while
we dedicated significant effort and compute to broadening the scope of
our evaluation, it remains limited to manipulation environments, which
currently form a major domain of application for VLAs. Further studies
on loco-manipulation and whole-body control ([NVIDIA et al.,
2025](#bib.bib17)) remain important directions for future work.
Moreover, the evaluation was designed with the constraint that the base
policy (in our case, $`\pi_{0.5}`$) would make non-trivial progress on
training tasks out of the box: for this reason, including tasks of
arbitrary complexity would be less informative. Finally, given the large
scale of our evaluation, and the number of diverse tasks required, it
remains constrained to simulated environments.

The main goal of this work is thus to contribute to the understanding of
mechanisms and trends of online self-improvement in dynamical systems.
We believe that our results represent a promising starting point for
future works, which can bootstrap off the simple and scalable RL recipes
we derived, and study the benefits of multi-task post-training at scale
on real hardware.

### Reproducibility statement

We ensure reproducibility by releasing code for our full training
pipeline at the URL listed at the end of
Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").
All data it uses is collected online, and no offline dataset is
necessary to reproduce results. Moreover, we thoroughly report training
details, hyperparameters and task splits in

## Appendix A Extended Related Work

Connections to LLM post-training.  A closely related pattern to the ones
we observe appears in LLM post-training. For instance, increasing the
diversity of instruction-finetuning tasks improves generalization to
held-out tasks ([Wei et al., 2022](#bib.bib70); [Iyer et al.,
2022](#bib.bib72); [Longpre et al., 2023](#bib.bib73); [Chung et al.,
2024](#bib.bib71)), with evidence of approximately log-linear scaling
with task coverage ([Longpre et al., 2023](#bib.bib73)) and stronger
gains for larger models ([Chung et al., 2024](#bib.bib71)). These works
primarily study supervised fine-tuning on fixed datasets, whereas we
consider *online self-improvement* through reinforcement learning and
study how its benefits scale with task diversity—a question that, to our
knowledge, has not been systematically investigated in robotics. More
directly, recent work comparing RL and supervised fine-tuning finds that
RL can generalize better to unseen task variants ([Chu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib28)) and better preserve previously acquired capabilities
during post-training ([Shenfeld et al., 2026](#bib.bib69)). These
observations relate to our results in
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"),
where FSFT similarly exhibits weaker generalization and degraded
performance on the training tasks compared to BoN.

## Appendix B A Taxonomy of Post-Training Algorithms

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 11: A taxonomy of a few VLA post-training approaches. Approaches
above the dashed line adopt a purely supervised objective for policy
extraction. We italicize the three approaches at the center of the
analysis in Sections
 [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Q1: Can we enable generalist improvement on training tasks? ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
and [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Q2: Do we see generalization beyond training tasks? ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").

Many algorithms have been proposed for finetuning pretrained generative
control policies, such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. We review
a few representative approaches and connect them to the two policy
improvement mechanisms identified in
[Section 3](#S3 "3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"):
direct policy adaptation and critic-guided refinement. As displayed in
Figure [11](#A2.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ Appendix B A Taxonomy of Post-Training Algorithms ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"),
we distinguish whether these methods use value estimates and perform
policy updates, and whether they use an unweighted supervised loss for
policy extraction. As FSFT, BoN and FSFT+BoN are already introduced in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"),
we focus on the remaining methods listed in
Figure [11](#A2.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ Appendix B A Taxonomy of Post-Training Algorithms ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").
This list is not meant to be exhaustive, but rather a representative
comparison of existing methods. For simplicity, we will absorb the task
conditioning in the state.

##### DPPO.

Diffusion Policy Policy Optimization ([Ren et al., 2025](#bib.bib49)) is
designed for generative policies involving a denoising process
$`a_{K:0}=(a_{K},\dots,a_{0})`$: starting from
$`a_{K}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I})`$, the generative model samples
$`a_{k-1}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s,a_{k},k,c)\quad\forall k=K,\dots,1`$,
until it arrives at the generated chunk $`a_{0}`$. DPPO applies
on-policy PPO to a two-layer MDP, embedding the inner denoising MDP
within the outer environment MDP. Policy gradients use tractable
Gaussian likelihoods at each denoising step, with environment-step
advantages estimated from on-policy rollouts and a state-value baseline.
This allows policy extraction through simple PPO updates. For
$`k=1,\dots,K`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\omega_{k}(\theta)=\frac{\bar{\pi}_{\theta}(a_{k-1}\mid s,a_{k},k)}{\bar{\pi}_{\theta_{\mathrm{EMA}}}(a_{k-1}\mid s,a_{k},k)},\quad\widehat{A}_{k}=\gamma_{\mathrm{den}}^{k-1}\widehat{A}^{\mathrm{env}},
``` |  | (8) |

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPPO}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=1}^{K}C_{\epsilon}\!\left(\omega_{k}(\theta),\widehat{A}_{k}\right)\right],
``` |  | (9) |

where $`\theta_{\mathrm{EMA}}`$ is an exponential moving average of the
policy parameters, $`\widehat{A}^{\mathrm{env}}`$ is estimated using
environment rewards and a learned value baseline,
$`\gamma_{\mathrm{den}}`$ discounts credit to earlier denoising
transitions and the PPO surrogate is
$`C_{\epsilon}(\omega,A)=\min\{\omega A,\operatorname{clip}(\omega,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)A\}`$.
We do not classify this method as leveraging critic-based guidance, as
the learned value function is not action-conditional, and is mostly used
for variance reduction rather than for evaluating actions. Nevertheless,
it updates the policy parameters, and thus performs direct policy
adaptation.

##### RECAP.

RL with Experience and Corrections via Advantage-conditioned Policies
([Intelligence et al., 2025a](#bib.bib50)) learns a state-only
distributional critic from Monte Carlo (MC) returns and converts
estimated advantages into binary conditioning labels. The policy is then
conditioned on these labels, and trained with a supervised flow matching
loss on both successful and unsuccessful trajectories. With the original
method’s undiscounted $`n`$-step estimation, the advantage and the
advantage labels for some state $`s_{0}`$ are expressed as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widehat{A}=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}r_{t+j}+V_{\eta}(s_{n})-V_{\eta}(s_{t}),\quad I_{t}=\mathbf{1}\{\widehat{A}>\varepsilon\},
``` |  | (10) |

for some threshold $`\varepsilon`$. As such, this method combines a form
of critic-based guidance (through advantage conditioning) with policy
adaptation through conditional behavior cloning.

##### AWR.

Advantage Weighted Regression ([Peng et al., 2019](#bib.bib25)) is an
actor-critic algorithm which avoids differentiation through the critic,
and updates the actor through a weighted supervised objective. Its early
instantiations rely on a critic trained through Monte Carlo return
estimation, but AWR has since been applied widely, e.g., with
temporal-difference critics in offline RL ([Park et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib66)). With the notation introduced in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"),
the advantage-weighted policy extraction objective is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\text{AWR}}(\theta)=-\,\mathbb{E}_{(s,a)\sim\mathcal{D}}\big[e^{\frac{\widehat{A}(s,a)}{\beta}}\log\pi_{\theta}(a|s)\big],
``` |  | (11) |

where $`\widehat{A}`$ is the advantage, often computed from
$`Q_{\psi}(s,a)`$, and $`\beta`$ is a temperature parameter that
recovers pure behavior cloning as $`\beta\to\infty`$.

##### PARL.

Policy Agnostic RL ([Mark et al., 2024](#bib.bib46)) trains a
state-action critic $`Q_{\psi}(s,a)`$, originally with either
IQL ([Kostrikov et al., 2022](#bib.bib9)) or Cal-QL ([Nakamoto et al.,
2023](#bib.bib65)), while policy extraction relies on two steps: action
optimization, and policy updates. The former consists of sampling action
candidates from the current policy, and leveraging first- and
zeroth-order optimization to approximately find
$`a^{\star}=\arg\max_{a}Q_{\psi}(s,a)`$ for each state and task in the
training batch. The latter simply encourages the policy to regress the
best candidate through unweighted behavior cloning (see
Equation [3](#S3.E3 "Equation 3 ‣ 3.2 Mechanisms for Generalist Improvement ‣ 3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")).
PARL is thus a close neighbor of FSFT+BoN; PARL optimizes over actions
at training-time instead of test-time, and trains its policy on both
successful and unsuccessful trajectories.

##### EXPO.

Expressive Policy Optimization  ([Dong et al., 2026a](#bib.bib43))
combines a critic trained through TD learning with a policy improvement
scheme that integrates an expressive base policy with a lightweight edit
policy. The edit policy is trained to maximize Q-values with a SAC-style
objective ([Haarnoja et al., 2018](#bib.bib67)), while the base policy
is updated according to a simple behavior cloning loss. Crucially, EXPO
integrates a BoN-like mechanism, both for selecting actions during
evaluation, and for computing TD targets. Thus, EXPO is also closely
connected to FSFT+BoN, mostly differing in the introduction of an edit
policy, and in the slightly different recipe used for value learning.

##### OGPO.

Off-Policy Generative Policy Optimization (OGPO) ([Patil et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22)) decouples the bi-level MDP formulation proposed in
[Ren et al. (2025)](#bib.bib49) and uses off-policy Q functions with
TD-learning for the environment MDP, while using on-policy PPO-style
policy extraction ([Schulman et al., 2017](#bib.bib41)) for the
denoising MDP of the generative control policy. For each replay state
from the replay buffer, OGPO rolls out a group of $`G`$ stochastic
actions to obtain group-relative advantages. This mitigates the need for
first-order optimization through the Q-functions and allows zeroth-order
updates by conditioning the likelihoods via the PPO objective keeping
the critics frozen during policy extraction:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widehat{A_{i}}=Q_{\mathrm{targ}}(s,a^{i,(0)})-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}Q_{\mathrm{targ}}(s,a^{j,(0)}),\quad\omega_{i}(\theta)=\prod_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a^{i,(k-1)}\mid s,a^{i,(k)},k)}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{slow}}}(a^{i,(k-1)}\mid s,a^{i,(k)},k)}
``` |  | (12) |

and

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OGPO}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D},\theta_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}C_{\epsilon}\!\left(\omega_{i}(\theta),\widehat{A_{i}}\right)\right].
``` |  | (13) |

Here, $`\widehat{A_{i}}`$ is the group relative advantage,
$`\omega_{i}(\theta)`$ is the annealed importance sampling ratio,
$`Q_{\mathrm{targ}}`$ is the EMA version of the online $`Q`$ function,
and similarly environment rollouts are conducted via
$`\pi_{\textsc{ema}}`$. Moreover,
$`(a^{i,(K)},\dots,a^{i,(0)})_{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s)`$
is a group of denoising sequences, and
$`\pi_{\theta}(a^{(k-1)}\mid s,a^{(k)})`$ denotes denoising-step
likelihoods. OGPO proposes an ODE-to-SDE conversion of pretrained flow
policies that allows the log probability updates on pretrained VLAs. Via
these likelihoods, $`\omega_{i}(\theta)`$ captures the importance ratio
between the denoising trajectories under current policy
$`\pi_{\theta}`$, and a slower-updating policy
$`\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{slow}}}`$ computed via a parameter
exponential-moving average. Finally, $`C_{\epsilon}`$ is a clipping
function
$`C_{\epsilon}(\omega,A):=\min\{\omega A,\operatorname{clip}(\omega,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)A\}`$
([Schulman et al., 2017](#bib.bib41)). Informally, this update
up-weights denoising sequences which lead to positive $`\hat{A}`$,
down-weights those which lead to negative $`\hat{A}`$, and incorporates
clipping $`C_{\epsilon}`$ to mitigate aggressive updates where the
policy is uncertain. OGPO also proposes two key stabilization
techniques: (1) a success buffer for FSFT on the base objective, and (2)
conservative advantages that stabilize the gradient updates through
underfit Q-functions in the beginning of RL-finetuning. Finally to
improve critic accuracy, OGPO incorporates Q-variance reduction which
averages the TD targets over $`N_{vr}`$ actions sampled from the actor.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{critic}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(Q(s_{t},a_{t})-\left(r_{t}+\gamma\frac{1}{N_{vr}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{vr}}Q(s_{t+1},a^{(i)}_{t+1})\right)\right)^{2}\right],a^{(i)}_{t+1}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t+1}).
``` |  | (14) |

## Appendix C Additional Empirical Results

### C.1 Generalist improvement on LIBERO: does generalization occur for completely novel tasks?

Figure 12: Value-based generalist improvement is limited when tasks are
loosely related. Performance of FSFT and BoN on training tasks (left)
and held-out tasks (right) in LIBERO as the training tasks grow in
number. The single-task lead of BoN reverses in larger multi-task
experiments, but FSFT exhibits substantial forgetting on held-out tasks,
unlike BoN.

We extend the evaluation reported in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
to LIBERO, in terms of performance on seen and unseen tasks. For
simplicity, we only consider the two most fundamental mechanisms out of
the three introduced in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").
When evaluated on seen tasks
(Figure [12](#A3.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ C.1 Generalist improvement on LIBERO: does generalization occur for completely novel tasks? ‣ Appendix C Additional Empirical Results ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"),
left), both direct policy adaptation (FSFT) and critic-guided refinement
(BoN) are generally able to improve success rates with respect to the
base policy. As observed in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"),
performance of multi-task models does not reach that of single-task
experts, particularly for BoN, which barely improves over the base
policy when trained over $`64`$ tasks.

The evaluation on unseen tasks
(Figure [12](#A3.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ C.1 Generalist improvement on LIBERO: does generalization occur for completely novel tasks? ‣ Appendix C Additional Empirical Results ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"),
right) is instead distinct from the one in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"),
and highlights the limits of generalization to unseen tasks. Here, the
degree of diversity of tasks is harder to control, and the variability
across tasks is higher. Unseen tasks often involve completely different
setups, motion patterns and goals compared to the training tasks. At the
scale we train on ($`N_{\mathrm{task}}\leq 64`$), generalization does
not emerge. Nevertheless, BoN remains preferable to FSFT, as it only
displays minimal forgetting.

### C.2 Extended Scaling Task Diversity Ablation

Figure 13: Diversify along the axis of desired generalization. Scaling
scenes of a single object (left two) or objects with one scene each
(right two), evaluated on unseen scenes and unseen objects. Each axis
transfers best along itself, and BoN scales better than FSFT, which
falls below the base policy on unseen objects. Mean over three seeds,
95% stratified bootstrap CIs.

We extend
Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.2 Q2: Do we see generalization beyond training tasks? ‣ 4 Generalist Improvement Scales With Task Diversity ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
by reporting trends for BoN and FSFT, and specify the task splits in
full. We scale the number of scenes of a single object,
$`\{1,4,8,16\}`$, and separately the number of objects, $`\{1,4,8\}`$,
with one scene each, evaluating both on eight held-out scenes of that
object and on eight unseen objects. MolmoSpaces has 18 objects, of which
we reserve 8 for evaluation, so at most 10 remain for training,
explaining why the object sweep has no 16-object split.
Table [1](#A3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ C.2 Extended Scaling Task Diversity Ablation ‣ Appendix C Additional Empirical Results ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
lists the splits.

As shown in
Figure [13](#A3.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ C.2 Extended Scaling Task Diversity Ablation ‣ Appendix C Additional Empirical Results ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"),
scaling scenes improves performance on unseen scenes by $`+36.5`$ pp for
BoN and $`+31`$ pp for FSFT, but does not transfer across objects: both
fall below the base policy there, although BoN recovers with more scenes
while FSFT does not. Scaling objects eventually transfers: BoN falls
below the base policy at $`1`$ and $`4`$ objects, but overtakes it at
$`8`$. At a matched budget of eight tasks each axis transfers best along
itself, by $`+6.6`$ pp on unseen scenes and $`+9.4`$ pp on unseen
objects. It is therefore beneficial to diversify along the axis of
desired generalization, though object diversity is more effective
overall.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

and
````
