### C.3 Allocating resources: data and compute

Figure 14: Post-training benefits from more data and more frequent
iterations. Final success rates for critic-guided refinement (BoN) on
LIBERO. Each subplot changes one hyperparameter: the number of episodes
collected per iteration (left), the number of gradient steps per
iteration (middle) and the number of iterations (right) over which a
data and compute budget is distributed. The other hyperparameters are
fixed per plot. $`1\times`$ marks the values used across the standard
experimental protocol described in
Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").
Collecting more data is beneficial with diminishing gains, while more
updates may be harmful; frequent iterations beat a single update phase
after data collection.

Online post-training involves three important design axes when it comes
to resource allocation: (i) how much data should be collected, (ii) how
many gradient steps should be applied and (iii) how data collection and
gradient updates should be interleaved. We thus consider these three
axes, and validate the main experimental protocol outlined in
Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
for BoN: post-training for $`10`$ iterations, each alternating data
collection ($`20`$ episodes per task) and model updates (100-500
gradient steps for the policy, $`100\times`$ for the critic). While we
present this ablation for BoN in LIBERO, we observed similar trends
across algorithms and environments.

As shown in the first column of
 [Figure 14](#A3.F14 "In C.3 Allocating resources: data and compute ‣ Appendix C Additional Empirical Results ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"),
we first study how performance changes with the amount of data collected
per iteration, while keeping the number of iterations and of gradient
steps fixed. We observe that in both single- and multi-task settings
(adopting the $`4`$-task split in this case), performance increases at a
decreasing rate. We thus adopt the highest budget which brings
significant benefits — $`20`$ episodes per task. The second column keeps
the number of episodes and iterations fixed instead, and ablates the
amount of compute that should be allocated to training. In this case, we
observe that more training is not always helpful, suggesting that the
underlying training dynamics of online RL are not entirely stable. For
these reasons, we settle on an intermediate budget. Finally, in the
third column, we keep the amount of data and compute fixed, and we
purely validate the number of iterations that should be applied. The
leftmost point of the plot collects all the data at once, and follows
this single data collection phase by a lengthy update phase, exhausting
the entire gradient budget. The rightmost point instead distributes data
and compute budgets across a large number of shorter iterations, each
collecting $`1/20`$th of the data and applying $`1/20`$th of the
gradient steps. Overall, we observe a gentle scaling trend which
plateaus at high iteration frequencies, suggesting that frequent
iterated online fine-tuning is beneficial. Accordingly, we post-train
our base model over $`10`$ iterations.

### C.4 Does a multi-task pre-trained critic transfer to new tasks?

Figure 15: Pretrained critic for accelerating value learning. A critic
pretrained on MolmoSpaces (64 tasks) starts higher than one trained from
scratch, but the gap closes within one iteration and then reverses, on
both unseen scenes (left) and unseen objects (right). Mean and 95%
stratified bootstrap CIs across three seeds.

A natural question in our setting is whether a critic pretrained on many
tasks can accelerate value learning on unseen ones. We compare BoN with
a critic pretrained on the MolmoSpaces (64 tasks) split against one
trained from scratch, evaluating on unseen scenes of the pretrained
critic’s training objects and on unseen objects.
Figure [15](#A3.F15 "Figure 15 ‣ C.4 Does a multi-task pre-trained critic transfer to new tasks? ‣ Appendix C Additional Empirical Results ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
shows that pretraining helps only initially: the pretrained critic
starts at a substantially higher success rate, but the gap closes in the
next iteration, after which it trails the randomly initialized critic on
both splits. These results indicate that pretrained critics offer little
benefit for accelerating value learning and can even be detrimental. One
possible explanation is a loss of plasticity in the pretrained critic,
though we leave the identification of the precise mechanism to future
work.

### C.5 Stability in direct policy adaptation

Figure 16: Learning rate ablation for FSFT. We sweep three learning
rates across four task splits: LIBERO (1 task), LIBERO (16 tasks),
MolmoSpaces (1 task), and MolmoSpaces (8 tasks). We evaluate performance
on the training tasks (In-Distr.) and on the validation tasks (OOD).
Bars show the mean over three seeds, with error bars denoting 95%
stratified bootstrap confidence.

FSFT has few hyperparameters, of which the learning rate is among the
most impactful. To assess its importance, we measure its influence on
in-distribution and out-of-distribution (OOD) performance across four
single- and multi-task splits: LIBERO (1 task), LIBERO (16 tasks),
MolmoSpaces (1 task), and MolmoSpaces (8 tasks). We sweep three learning
rates, $`\{2.5\cdot 10^{-6},\,2.5\cdot 10^{-5},\,2.5\cdot 10^{-4}\}`$,
over three seeds each, leaving all other hyperparameters unchanged.
Figure [16](#A3.F16 "Figure 16 ‣ C.5 Stability in direct policy adaptation ‣ Appendix C Additional Empirical Results ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
presents the results. The smallest value, $`2.5\cdot 10^{-6}`$, degrades
in-distribution performance, while the largest, $`2.5\cdot 10^{-4}`$, is
detrimental OOD. These results suggest that the learning rate mediates a
trade-off between in-distribution and OOD performance. The middle value,
$`2.5\cdot 10^{-5}`$, balances the two, and we adopt it as the default
in our FSFT experiments.

### C.6 Number of action candidates $`N`$ in Best-of-$`N`$

Figure 17: Impact of the number of candidates $`N`$ in Best-of-$`N`$ on
performance. Success rate of BoN on each of the four single-task
MolmoSpaces runs as $`N`$ grows. On average, performance grows with
$`N`$ and peaks at $`N=32`$, though the gains over $`N\in\{8,16\}`$ are
marginal. We report mean and 95% stratified bootstrap CIs over three
seeds.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Table 2: BoN inference cost. Wall-clock time of one Best-of-$`N`$ step
on a single GH200 GPU, relative to $`N{=}1`$.

Beyond critic learning, Best-of-$`N`$ introduces a single
hyperparameter: the number of sampled actions $`N`$. At each step it
draws $`N`$ candidates
$`\{a_{t}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}\sim\pi_{\theta}(s_{t},c)`$, scores them, and
executes $`a_{t}^{\star}=\arg\max_{i}Q_{\psi}(s_{t},a_{t}^{i},c)`$.
Larger $`N`$ gives the critic more candidates to choose from, at the
cost of slower inference. To assess the impact of $`N`$ on performance,
we ablate $`N\in\{2,4,8,16,32\}`$ on four single-task MolmoSpaces runs.
As shown in
Figure [17](#A3.F17 "Figure 17 ‣ C.6 Number of action candidates 𝑁 in Best-of-𝑁 ‣ Appendix C Additional Empirical Results ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"),
performance roughly grows with $`N`$ on all tasks and peaks on average
at $`N=32`$, which we adopt as our default. The gains are diminishing,
however: $`N=32`$ improves only marginally over $`N\in\{8,16\}`$.

[Table 2](#A3.T2 "In C.6 Number of action candidates 𝑁 in Best-of-𝑁 ‣ Appendix C Additional Empirical Results ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
reports the wall-clock time of one BoN step as a function of $`N`$. Our
default $`N=32`$ costs $`3.49\times`$ the time of $`N=1`$, against
$`1.59\times`$ for $`N=8`$, which offers a better balance between
performance and inference cost. Since our experiments run in simulation,
we keep $`N=32`$ to prioritize performance; on a real robot, $`N=8`$
would likely be preferable.

## Appendix D Experimental Details

### D.1 Environments and Task Splits

This section describes the environments we use and how we construct task
splits. In all of our experiments, we utilize two benchmarks: LIBERO-90
and MolmoSpaces. LIBERO is a widely used manipulation benchmark, whereas
MolmoSpaces offers precise control over task diversity, which makes it
better suited to studying generalization. We use its pick suite, which
exposes 18 objects with 55–56 scenes each, allowing us to vary scene and
object diversity independently.

Task IDs are shown in the lower-left corner of each frame.

Studying multi-task training and generalization requires training splits
of increasing size but comparable difficulty, together with held-out
tasks. For MolmoSpaces, we first estimate the initial success rate of
each task by rolling out 48 episodes with the base policy. From these we
construct five training splits of 1, 4, 16, 64, and 144 tasks, each a
superset of the smaller ones, with a mean initial success rate near
$`30\%`$. A split of $`k^{2}`$ tasks contains $`k`$ objects with $`k`$
scenes each. We evaluate each training split on two held-out sets. The
first contains eight unseen scenes of every object the split was trained
on, so each split is tested only on new scenes of its own objects. The
second, shared by all splits, contains eight scenes each of six objects
that appear in no training split.
Table [3](#A4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ D.1 Environments and Task Splits ‣ Appendix D Experimental Details ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
lists the resulting splits together with their objects and the initial
success rates, and
Figures [18](#A4.F18 "Figure 18 ‣ D.1 Environments and Task Splits ‣ Appendix D Experimental Details ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"), [19](#A4.F19 "Figure 19 ‣ D.1 Environments and Task Splits ‣ Appendix D Experimental Details ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement"),
and [20](#A4.F20 "Figure 20 ‣ D.1 Environments and Task Splits ‣ Appendix D Experimental Details ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
visualize the tasks.

We construct the LIBERO splits in the same way, estimating initial
success rates from 48 rollouts on 89 of the 90 tasks, and again running
the single-task split on four tasks. LIBERO is smaller than MolmoSpaces,
so its splits cannot be balanced as tightly: mean initial success rate
ranges from $`23.4\%`$ to $`27.0\%`$. A further 25 tasks are held out to
measure generalization.
Table [4](#A4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ D.1 Environments and Task Splits ‣ Appendix D Experimental Details ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
lists the splits and their initial success rates.

### D.2 Implementation Details

Common Setup.   All methods start from the same pretrained $`\pi_{0.5}`$
checkpoint, i.e., pi05_libero on LIBERO and pi05_droid_jointpos on
MolmoSpaces, and share the same data collection loop. As in the released
checkpoint, the policy sees only camera images and the language
instruction; we verified that omitting proprioceptive state helps. Each
iteration begins with a collection phase, in which the policy collects
20 episodes per task into a replay buffer; training then proceeds and
differs by method. After the last iteration, a final evaluation phase
begins. Collection and evaluation both use an exponential moving average
of the policy parameters for stability. The policy outputs a chunk of 15
actions (10 actions on LIBERO) but executes only the first 5 before
being queried again. We nonetheless store one sample per environment
step, pairing each observation with the full action chunk executed from
that step onward, stitched across consecutive queries rather than taken
from a single predicted chunk. The buffer is FIFO and sampled uniformly.

FSFT.   FSFT stores only successful episodes and fine-tunes all policy
parameters, i.e., VLM backbone, action expert, and vision encoder, with
the standard $`\pi_{0.5}`$ flow-matching loss.

BoN.   BoN keeps the VLA’s parameters frozen and instead learns a
$`Q`$-function conditioned on observations and action chunks. At every
query, it samples $`N{=}32`$ candidate chunks with independent initial
noise and executes the one maximizing the minimum over the critic’s
ensemble, both during data collection and at evaluation. The critic
never sees raw images as it takes the mean-pooled final-layer token
embeddings of the policy’s backbone, the proprioceptive state, and the
flattened action chunk as input. Since the policy is frozen, this
embedding is computed once at collection time and cached, which makes
critic training substantially faster. We use a time-to-success reward
($`-1`$ per step, $`0`$ on success), with episodes terminating only on
success and time limits treated as truncation. We train $`Q`$ and $`V`$
on all collected episodes with $`H`$-step TD targets from slowly updated
target networks: the $`H`$ discounted rewards accumulated over the
chunk, plus $`\gamma^{H}`$ times the bootstrapped value of the state
reached at its end. Because $`V`$ regresses $`Q`$ at buffer actions
rather than at a maximum or an upper expectile, this is a SARSA-style
evaluation of the data-collecting policy.

OGPO.   Our implementation of OGPO mostly follows the design choices
specified in the original paper (([Patil et al., 2026](#bib.bib22))).
However, we make some additional design choices and modifications to
adapt it to fine-tune $`\pi_{0.5}`$. Specifically, we make the following
design choices for our runs:

- •
  Critic: Our implementation parametrizes the state-action value
  function using a BroNet residual MLP and uses an ensemble of 10
  critics ([Patil et al., 2026](#bib.bib22)). The critics are aggregated
  by randomly sub-sampling two critics and then picking the minimum
  among the two.
- •
  Critic Update: The critic is learned by regressing on a TD target with
  Q-variance reduction expressed in Equation
  [14](#A2.E14 "Equation 14 ‣ OGPO. ‣ Appendix B A Taxonomy of Post-Training Algorithms ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").
  At every training step, this critic receives two gradient updates: one
  on a batch of transitions sampled from the replay buffer, and one on a
  batch sampled only from successful episodes. This success oversampling
  helps amplify the sparse reward signal.
- •
  Policy Updates: Policy updates are performed using the group relative
  advantages as per Equation
  [12](#A2.E12 "Equation 12 ‣ OGPO. ‣ Appendix B A Taxonomy of Post-Training Algorithms ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")
  and Equation
  [13](#A2.E13 "Equation 13 ‣ OGPO. ‣ Appendix B A Taxonomy of Post-Training Algorithms ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").
  Additionally, policy updates also use conservative advantages and BC
  loss on transitions from successful episodes for stability.
- •
  BoN: During collection rounds, we generate a set of $`N=32`$ candidate
  chunks using SDE sampling and execute the one with the highest
  Q-value. We aggregate the Q-function for this using the same
  aggregation strategy described above. Evaluation uses $`N=1`$.
- •
  Training: In experiments with OGPO, the backbone is frozen and only
  the action expert is trained.

The other design choices and exact hyperparameters used in our
implementation are specified in
Table [5](#A4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ D.3 Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix D Experimental Details ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement").

AWR.   The training pipeline of AWR is mostly the same pipeline as OGPO.
The sole difference is in the policy training objective. AWR uses a
weighted supervised loss (see
Equation [3](#S3.E3 "Equation 3 ‣ 3.2 Mechanisms for Generalist Improvement ‣ 3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")).
The AWR weights are computed using the group relative advantages
computed from the critic and normalize the advantages by dividing by the
group’s standard deviation. The BC loss on successful transitions from
OGPO is retained with the same weight.

FSFT+BoN.   FSFT+BoN collects data with BoN and additionally fine-tunes
the expert head of the policy on the successful transitions of the
shared buffer. The critic training pipeline and collection strategy are
the same as OGPO.

### D.3 Hyperparameters

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Table 5: Hyperparameters. *Training budget*: each run performs $`M`$
collection rounds of $`K`$ episodes per task, with the given number of
gradient steps per round (single-task / multi-task). *Tuned weights*:
whether the full VLA or only the action expert is fine-tuned. *Trained
on*: whether the SFT loss uses only successful episodes. *Update
interval*: critic steps per policy update. *Bootstrap*: SARSA uses the
next action stored in the buffer, TD uses an action sampled from the
current policy. Critic-based methods use a replay buffer of 1M
transitions (2M for OGPO on the 144-task split). BoN and OGPO run for 10
collection rounds, except on the 144-task split, where we extend it to
15 rounds because performance had not yet plateaued. FSFT, in contrast,
plateaus early and then slightly declines, so 10 rounds was enough.

### D.4 Evaluation Protocol

In this section we describe the evaluation protocol. On both LIBERO and
MolmoSpaces we evaluate each policy in distribution and on unseen tasks.
For LIBERO, the unseen set comprises 25 tasks; for MolmoSpaces, eight
unseen scenes of objects from the 144-task split and six unseen objects
(see
Appendix [D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Environments and Task Splits ‣ Appendix D Experimental Details ‣ Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement")).
Our metric throughout is success rate.

During training, the in-distribution success rate is measured on the 20
episodes the policy collects per task in each round, so no extra
mid-evaluation rollouts are needed. After the last training phase, we
run a separate evaluation phase of 32 episodes per task, both in
distribution and on unseen tasks. We repeat every experiment with three
seeds and report the mean success rate over seeds, together with 95%
stratified bootstrap confidence intervals computed with
rliable ([Agarwal et al., 2021](#bib.bib31)).

### D.5 Computational Resources

Our experiments ran on nodes with four NVIDIA GH200 GPUs each. A
single-task run took about 2-5 hours of wall-clock time depending on the
task, and runs on the largest multi-task splits took 200 hours.
